abstract: Spontaneously transformed mouse ovarian surface epithelial cell line ID8 generates a syngeneic mouse model, recapitulating the primary and metastatic stages of the malignancy hence, frequently used in pre-clinical evaluation. Due to inherent phenotypic plasticity, primary and metastatic tumors show contrasting phenotypic features dictated by the tissue niche. To address the tumor heterogeneity within the model we stratified it into a specific molecular subtype, which would provide an accurate setting for interpretation of experimental data. Stratification was performed on ID8 cell line and ID8 generated xenografts based on immunostaining, live cell imaging, histopathology, transcriptomics and proteomics. Tumor microenvironment (TME) investigation for each xenograft was done through flow cytometry analysis. ID8 cells present epithelial/mesenchymal (E/M) phenotype. Phenotypic plasticity retention in them causes class switching of ID8 cells in response to niche alteration, from E/M (in culture) to intermediate epithelial (iE) in orthotopic tumors while intermediate mesenchymal (iM) in subcutaneous tumors. Metastasis of ID8 primary tumor resulted into differentiated mesenchymal phenotype in ascites while differentiated epithelial phenotype in secondary intestinal tumors. Immune profiling of primary and secondary xenografts revealed differences in immune repertoire of tumors, highlighting subcutaneous tumor model to be inappropriate as compared to orthotopic model. Local tissue niche modulates the phenotype of tumors generated, transitioning through intermediate states towards a final commitment to either an epithelial or mesenchymal state that recapitulates the reported class switching in patient tumors. During disease progression, such heterogeneity of tumor cells at different niche(s) and their cross-talks with discrete TME at each site, will pose challenges for effective therapy. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1038/s41598-025-18264-8.

Methods
Cell culture
A4 cell line previously established from HGSC patient ascites was cultured as reported
14
. OVCAR3 (from the NCCS cell repository) and OVCA420 (a kind gift from Prof. Clements, TRI, Australia) were obtained and grown in RPMI-1640 supplemented with 10% FBS. ID8 cells were purchased from ATCC and grown in Dulbecco’s Modified Essential Medium supplemented with 10% FBS. All cell lines were maintained in a humidified incubator at 37 °C under 5% CO2 atmosphere.
Immunostaining, live cell imaging (wound healing) image acquisition and quantification
Immunostaining was performed as described previously
14
. Briefly, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde, permeabilized with chilled methanol, blocked with 10% goat serum, incubated with primary antibody, followed by secondary antibody (Table S1) performed in triplicates (three individual experiments with cells of different passages and three technical replicates with the cells of same passage). Images were acquired (60 images from 5 fields per replicate) on Olympus FV3000 confocal microscope at 63× magnification; mean fluorescence intensity (MFI/ area) calculated on ImageJ. Live cell imaging for wound healing was performed as described previously
16
. Briefly, a scratch generated on a confluent cell layer was imaged for healing in serum-free medium at 37 °C, 5% CO2 atmosphere over 48 h using an inverted laser scanning confocal fluorescence microscope (LPSS5, Leica Microsystems), performed in triplicates (individual experiments with cells of different passages and 3 replicates with cells of same passage).
Xenograft establishment and Qupath based quantification
6–8-week-old C57BL6 female mice, provided by NCCS Animal Experimentation Facility, Pune were housed in IVCs (2–4 mice per cage) according to the guidelines provided by Institutional Animal Ethics Committee [IAEC; EAF/2023/B-436(I)]. Primary tumors were developed subcutaneously (ID8-sc: 5 × 10
6
ID8 cells on right and left flank, n = 3) or orthotopically (ID8-ortho: 2 × 10
6
ID8 cells intra-bursal on right ovary, n = 5). A latency of ~ 4 months from date of injection for both was noted; ID8-ortho further progressed to metastasis. Temporal harvesting of peritoneal tumor ascites was performed 3 times under aseptic conditions (ID8-asc tap1, ID8-asc tap2, ID8-asc tap3) using a syringe and needle. H and E-stained images of xenografts were acquired, for 4 different mice of the same batch on Zeiss Axio Imager Z2 microscope using a 0.5 × 0.5 cm transparent grid, selecting upper right corner section in each grid, at 10 × and 40 × magnification. Number of fields counted were variable for each sample because of tumor size (details in Additional File
2
). Training of Qupath algorithm
17
was achieved in pre-stratified HGSC patient tumors (13 patients) and tested on a set of unstratified patient tumors (8 patients) (details in Additional File
2
). The trained Qupath-based stratification was then extended to annotation and quantification of ID8 tumors.
Sampling, RNA extraction, sequencing and data analysis
RNA extraction and library preparation from 3 biological replicates of ID8 cells (control) and tumors (sample) was performed by MedGenome Labs Ltd employing modified NEBNext RNA Ultra II directional protocol; total RNA sequencing performed on Illumina HiSeqX (60 M, 2 × 150 bp reads/sample). Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA software v 2023.2)
18
,
19
was applied to detect enriched MSigDB mouse gene sets, ~ 1000 “gene set” type permutations were performed with significant differentially expressed genes (
p
< 0.05, Fold Change > 2& < − 2), which returned pathways displayed as enrichment maps (
p
< 0.05)
20
.
Proteomics and data analysis
Trypsin-digested protein preparations from 3 biological replicates of ID8 cells (control) and tumors (sample) were used to acquire mass spectra in positive ionization mode on Orbitrap Fusion Mass Spectrometer (Thermo-Fischer Scientific), and data subjected to label-free quantification (LFQ) in triplicate (ID8 cells of same passages and tumors from 3 different mice of same batch), as described previously
21
, using Max Quant (v1.6.17.0) with
Mus musculus
proteome (Uniprot ID- UP000000589). LFQ > ratio counts 1 were selected to return quantified peptides from different protein groups, for triplicates (ID8 cells of same passages and tumors from 3 different mice of same batch). These were subjected to Perseus (v1.6.14.0) in triplicate, to identify significantly expressed proteins based on LFQ intensity (student ‘t’ test;
p
≤ 0.05, > 2 unique + razor peptides with sequence coverage percentage > 10%). This analysis resolved common and exclusive proteins (expressed in both or either control or test samples respectively) as represented in volcano plots (log2 fold-change ≥ 2 or ≤ − 2 vs. log10
p
> 1.3). Further pathway enrichment analysis was achieved using ClueGO (v2.5.10) as a Cytoscape (3.9.1) plugin
22
with GO-biological process, GO (Cellular Component, Immune System Process, Molecular Function), KEGG
23
, Reactome (Pathways and Reactions) considering minimum 5 genes per term, Kappa score 0.4 cutoffs,
p
≤ 0.05 for triplicates..
ImmuCellAI-based deconvolution and flow cytometry for tumor microenvironment (TME) composition of tumors
Immune Cell Abundance Identifier-mouse tool
24
was used to deconvolute normalized read counts of ID8 tumor transcriptomes into 36 immune cells against mouse reference expression profiles and marker gene sets for triplicates (ID8 cells of same passages and tumors from 3 different mice of same batch). For flow cytometry based estimations, tumors were dissociated enzymatically using collagenase while ascites was processed for RBC lysis. Staining was performed as described
25
. Briefly, single cell suspensions were processed for live/dead staining, blocked for 20 min followed by surface staining for 30 min with fluorophore tagged antibodies. Intracellular staining samples fixed and permeabilized for 30 min using 1 × Fix/Perm buffer followed by intracellular staining for 60 min with fluorochrome tagged antibodies (Table S2) for triplicates (Tumors from different mice of same batch and no. of batches were 3). Samples were acquired on Cytek Aurora on the same day. Compensation was performed on SpectroFlov3.0. Gating and UMAP plots were prepared on OMIQ software from Dotmatics (
www.omiq.ai
,
www.dotmatics.com
).
ID8 irradiation and ecadherin expression quantification
ID8 cells were grown till confluency and irradiated at 50 Gy. After 3 days of recovery Ecadherin expression was quantified through flow cytometry in comparison with non-irradiated ID8 cells in triplicates (3 individual experiments with different cell passages and 3 replicates with cells of same passage).
Data analysis, statistics, and graphical representation
All experiments were performed in triplicates (3 individual experiments with samples in triplicates for each experiment). Data significance was assigned based on unpaired Student ‘t’ test and Mann–Whitney Test. p

body:
Introduction
High-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSC) presents with the worst prognosis and patient outcomes amongst all gynecological malignancies in India
1
. Challenges in HGSC include late detection, asymptomatic progression and a high degree of tumor heterogeneity that necessitates targeted therapy and personalized medicine. PARP inhibitors have emerged as a frontline monotherapy followed by cytoreductive surgery and as maintenance therapy for BRCA1/2 deficient tumors but have limited efficacy in improving survival in other patient groups
2
–
4
. To develop precise treatments, we need to test them in animal models that closely mimic the complexity and heterogeneity of tumors found in patients. The ID8 syngeneic mouse model for HGSC was established as a spontaneously transformed mouse ovarian surface epithelial (MOSE) cell line that is extensively used in pre-clinical studies, especially to elucidate tumor-immune cross-talks for immunotherapy
5
,
6
. However, a deeper phenotypic characterization of this model in terms of representing a specific HGSC subtype is as yet not reported
7
–
9
. This is crucial since the plasticity of tumor cells that leads to modulation of cellular phenotypes (epithelial, E; mesenchymal, M; intermediate epithelial, iE; intermediate mesenchymal, iM; Hybrid, E/M) is increasingly being associated with treatment outcomes
10
. Importantly, the E/M hybrid state is regarded as a metastable phenotype that may divert lineages towards either E or M through their respective intermediate iE/iM states facilitating mesenchymal to epithelial transition (MET) and epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT) respectively
11
. Additionally, intratumor heterogeneity resulting from cross-talks between cancer stem-like cells and the tumor microenvironment may well remain a confounding feature in therapy
12
. Previously, molecular classification of HGSC tumors have reported distinct subtypes based on their expression patterns, extent of phenotypic plasticity and functional/behavioral diversity
13
. Earlier, applying a gene expression module enrichment-based strategy, we resolved three HGSC subtypes including,
Class1/E/CCM (Epithelial tumors associated with cooperative cellular migration),
Class2/M/EMT (mesenchymal tumors that metastasize through EMT) and
Class3/E/M hybrid (tumors with mixed epithelial and mesenchymal features capable of both CCM- and EMT-driven migration)
14
.
Further, we clinically validated expression of E-Cadherin (E-cadh), TCF21 and PARP1 in Class1 (CCM/E) tumors and Slug, AnnexinA2 (Anxa2) and hyaluronic acid in Class2 (EMT/M) tumors. Class 3 (E/M hybrid) tumors were either double positive (DP) or double negative (DN) for these biomarkers
13
,
15
. Clinical validation also revealed ‘class switching’, involving phenotypic plasticity and altered marker expression in response in different tumor niches and/or treatment. These observations together was the rationale to initiate extensive histopathological and molecular assessments to understand the extent of phenotypic heterogeneity, plasticity and stemness in the ID8 syngeneic mouse model. This would assign the model a precise, subtype-specific perspective for interpretation of experimental data towards its application in therapeutic evaluation.

Results
ID8 cells express phenotypic and functional markers of Epithelial-CCM as well as Mesenchymal-EMT classes
An evaluation of class-specific marker expression in ID8 cells and class-representative cell line models (Class1/E/CCM—OVCAR3, Class2/EMT/M—A4, Class3/E/M hybrid—OVCA420; 14) revealed co-expression of CCM (E-cadh, TCF21) and EMT markers (Slug, Anxa2) in ID8 cells, accompanied by co-localization of the transcription factors TCF21 and Slug (Fig.
1
a,b) (Figure S1a). We further performed a real-time, live cell imaging-based comparison of cell migration, which revealed rapid wound healing in A4 and ID8 cells (38 h and 42 h respectively) (Additional Movies 1 & 3) and significantly lower capabilities in OVCAR3 and OVCA420 cells (Fig.
1
c) (Figure S1b) (Additional Movies 2 & 4). Specifically, A4 cells display single cell migration (EMT) as well as sheet-like movement (active CCM, aCCM), OVCAR3 cells mediate wound healing through extensive proliferation at the wound edge (passive CCM, pCCM), OVCA420 migrate collectively through aCCM
16
. ID8 cells however, displayed a mixed modality of migration with leader cells at the wound edge acquiring a spindle-shape that facilitates EMT, while the remaining population retained an epithelial phenotype and migrates in aCCM mode (Additional Movie 3). These phenotypic and functional features suggest ID8 cells to reside in a mixed or transitioning state that aligns with the Class3/Mixed/E/M hybrid phenotype. We further tested the suggested plasticity under conditions of stress (50 Gy irradiation). Indeed, expression of the epithelial marker E-cadh was enhanced post irradiation, validating metastability of E/M state and shift to an epithelial phenotype (Fig.
1
d).

Microenvironmental cues manifest the in-situ cell phenotype of ID8 xenografts
We further examined the growth characteristics of ID8 primary xenografts generated either on intra-bursal (orthotopic, ID8-ortho) or subcutaneous (ID8-sc) implantation to understand differential in situ behavior(s). While ID8-sc tumor growth was restricted to the site of injection, ID8-ortho recapitulated classical clinical disease progression including metastasis to the peritoneum to generate tumor ascites (ID8-asc) and secondary tumors in the intestine (ID8-met_int), stomach, liver, kidneys, pancreas, omentum, spleen, heart and lungs that advance to aggregate in the peritoneum (Fig.
1
e) (Figure S2). A similar latency of ~ 150 days was observed in either primary xenograft (data not shown), identified as time to development of peritoneal tumor ascites (ID8-asc-Tap1) in ID8-ortho, or palpable tumors in ID8-sc. Histopathological assessment of primary xenografts and intestinal metastases (ID8-met_int) revealed a discrete tumor architecture; ID8-ortho and ID8-met_int were populated with epithelial cells demarcated by well-defined cell boundaries and large, isodiametric, densely stained nuclei, while ID8-sc predominantly harbored spindle-shaped mesenchymal-like cells with uneven boundaries and densely stained nuclei (Fig.
1
f).
Our earlier immunohistochemistry-based clinical validation of the three predicted HGSC tumor classes had revealed some interesting features, (i) the E/M hybrid class was subtyped as either double-positive (DP) or double-negative (DN) for expression of the six stratification markers, and (ii) Metastases- and/or chemotherapy-induced stress triggers class switching
13
,
15
. Towards a deeper histopathological evaluation, we trained a machine-learning classifier, Qupath to quantify epithelial, stromal, necrotic, vascular areas and tumor infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) in H & E-stained tumor sections of the HGSC patients stratified into either E, M or DP subtypes that represented the training set (Additional File
2
-Table 1). Further deployment of this classifier to DN tumors (representing the test set), achieved their resolution into specific E/M/E/M (DP) sub-types thereby adding an independent and unbiased parameter into our stratification. Such development was a necessary pre-requisite and provided a tool to facilitate precise sub-typing of ID8 xenografts. Deployment of trained Qupath identified highest enrichment of epithelial cells in ID8-met_int tumors, high frequencies of epithelial and vascular elements, and TILs in ID8-ortho tumors, while stromal elements were more emphasized in ID8-sc (Fig.
1
g–h). TIL infiltration levels in ID8-ortho versus ID8-sc tumors indicate scarcity of immune populations in ID8-sc tumors, proving it to be a non-responsive and irrelevant site for immune therapy testing unlike ID8-ortho and ID8-met_Int. Further PCA analysis of all histopathological features to group samples into discrete subtypes led to alignment of ID8-ortho and ID8-met_int tumors with E/CCM samples, while ID8-sc tumors clustered with the M/EMT group (Fig.
1
i). This collectively suggests that the hybrid (E/M) state of ID8 cells grown in vitro metastable and can be driven towards different phenotypes by the niche in which it establishes a tumor.
Molecular components of xenografts display considerable tumor heterogeneity that reflects on intrinsic cellular plasticity despite niche-triggered lineage commitments
Towards further molecular resolution of the phenotypic differences, we compared the transcriptomes and proteomes of ID8 cells grown in vitro with their primary xenografts, 3 consecutive tappings of metastatic tumor ascites (ID8-asc-Tap1, ID8-asc-Tap2, ID8-asc-Tap3) and ID8-met_int; proteome profiles specifically emphasized the discrete molecular underpinnings of each sample (Fig.
2
a). Comparison between the two primary xenografts at the transcript level assigned an epithelial signature to ID8-ortho characterized by retention of pluripotency and self-renewal capacity. Pathways that could assign terminal differentiation towards epithelial lineage were absent. At the protein level we observed enrichment of immune regulation and stemness, implying ID8-ortho to be immunologically infiltrated and transitioning from E/M hybrid (ID8 cells) to an induced epithelial phenotype (Fig.
2
b,c) (Table S3). On the other hand, ID8-sc was assigned mesenchymal phenotype with upregulated stemness at transcript and protein level, but there was no enrichment of immune response pathways, indicative of the immunologically inactive state (Fig.
2
d,e) (Table S7) (Table S11) (Figure S4a-b). However, despite this commitment to epithelial and mesenchymal lineages, continuing co-expression of epithelial transcripts and proteins suggest partial retention of the inherent parental cell plasticity. This presents a conundrum that can be resolved through understanding and assigning of intermediate states iE and iM in ID8-ortho and ID8-sc respectively. Such intermediate states are more stably represented in cell cultures and considered transient in situ
26
. Conclusively, the above molecular signatures signify divergence of expression patterns and possibly gene regulatory mechanisms from the E/M hybrid ID8 cells to iE and iM states in orthotopic versus subcutaneous niches respectively. Retention of this plasticity may be a requisite for further metastases and disease progression.

Paired comparisons of differential expression during disease progression between ID8-ortho, ID8-asc (ID8-asc Tap1& ID8-asc Tap2) and ID8-met_int revealed the following:
ID8-ortho versus ID8-asc analyses reaffirmed the iE phenotype in the former due to re-enrichment of pathways that indicate a shift towards epithelial state with retention of stromal and stem cell signatures, while ID8-asc was assigned a mesenchymal signature as indicated by the highly enriched pathways associated to stromal cells, cell motility and wound healing. Other less enriched pathways signifying epithelial phenotype are a result of spheroids, commonly found in ascites. Protein enrichment resulted into mmune responsiveness dominated by antigen presentation and lymphocyte activation pathways (Fig.
3
a,b) (Figure S3a) (Figures S4c,S4d) (Table S4, Table S8 & Table S12). Enriched common proteins showed a mix of pathways from ID8-asc and ID8-ortho (Fig.
3
c).
Comparing two consecutive ID8-asc (ID8-asc Tap1; ID8-asc Tap2) with ID8-met_int expression assigned a distinct E phenotype to ID8-met_int comprising of epithelial cell organogenesis and differentiation, that explicitly indicated a lineage commitment towards E phenotype unlike ID8-ortho, retaining pluripotency and few mesenchymal features. Proteomic and transcriptomic profiles reassigned an EMT signature to ID8-asc Tap1 and ID8-asc Tap2 that also was associated with lineage commitment and stem cell differentiation. Expression of related proteins re-emphasized the earlier dominance of antigen presentation and T cell response in ID8-asc tumors (Fig.
3
d,e) (Figure S3b, Figures S4e & S4f.) (Table S5, Table S9 & Table S13). Very little commonality of expression between the two tumor types was noted (Fig.
3
f). Conclusively, ID8-met_int tumors could be assigned a definitive differentiated E phenotype whereas ID8-asc M phenotype.
Analyses of ID8-met_int versus ID8-ortho expression aligned both xenografts towards an E phenotype marked with highly enriched pathways associated with epithelial cell organogenesis in ID8-met_Int, that indicated, higher extent of epithelialization in ID8-met_int tumors. ID8-ortho expressed few mesenchymal elements (Fig.
3
g,h) (Figure S3c, Figures S4g,S4h) (Table S6, Table S10 & Table S14). Common proteins indicated immune infiltration in both tumors (Fig.
3
i), which were key regulatory proteins in ID8-met_int as an inflammatory signature. Together, this suggests ID8-ortho to represent a less differentiated (iE) state, whereas ID8-met_int represents a differentiated E phenotype.

The immune cell composition varies at different niches
Besides the above definitive resolution of differential phenotypic presentation of tumor cells in response to various niches, variable immune involvement at each tumor site was revealed by the histopathology-based QuPath analysis. Strikingly, the extent of TIL infiltration in the tumor microenvironment (TME) was noted to be highest in ID8-met_int (E), followed by ID8-ortho (iE) and lowest in ID8-sc (iM). Molecular analyses further emphasized differential associations of tumor phenotype with specificity of antigen presentation and T cell responses, immune infiltration associated neutrophil trap formation, innate immune system activation, MHC I Ag processing and presentation, inflammation etc. (Fig.
3
a,d,g). To further resolve specific immune cell variations, we applied two approaches -
Deconvolution of transcriptomic data using an ImmuAI algorithm that assigns an enrichment score signifying abundance of immune subsets in tumors (Figures.S5a, S5b) and
Resolution of enriched immune cell populations at different tumor niches through dimensional reduction of flow cytometry profiles of TME cell components (gating strategy in Figure S6).
Transcriptome deconvolution of primary tumors (ID8-sc; ID8-ortho) revealed ID8-sc to be abundant in classical and plasmodial dendritic cells DCs (cDCs, pDCs), follicular and memory B cells, while ID8-ortho displayed abundant infiltration of M1 and M2 types of macrophages, mast cells, neutrophils and eosinophils indicating it to be better inflamed with both innate and adaptive immune responses (Figure S5). Surface and intracellular marker profiling in both primary tumors through spectral flow cytometry suggested scarcity of anti-tumorigenic cell types (cytotoxic CD8-T cells expressing perforin, NK, M1 type macrophages) with pro-tumorigenic Tregs being enriched in ID8-sc over ID8-ortho tumors. Strikingly, pro-tumorigenic MDSCs were more frequent in ID8-sc indicating better survival of ID8 cells within the TME. Thus, the immune landscape of ID8-ortho signifies potential of cytotoxic response with Tregs under control, while that of ID8-sc recapitulates desert immune phenotype with poor cytotoxic response (Fig.
4
a–e).

Discussion
Considerable current interest is focused on the, intermediate E/M hybrid state of tumor cells that await ‘to grow’ or ‘to go’ cues from the microenvironment and attain an E or M phenotype through MET or EMT respectively
27
. Such inherent plasticity ensures tumor cell survival under different conditions of stress
21
. Earlier reports have identified this E/M state through discrete scRNA, trancriptomic and chromatin profiles, while co-expression of E-cadherin and vimentin along with a functional association of efficient wound healing has also been reported
28
,
29
. Herein, we identified that ID8 cells represent anE/M hybrid state under steady-state culture. This provided us an opportunity to further characterize and understand the in in situ behavior of this metastable stateduring disease progression. Our earlier studies established that the Class 3/Mixed HGSC subtype identified by us earlier in clinical tumors
13
,
15
is likely to emerge from an E/M hybrid state, which responds to molecular signals from the niche to define lineage commitment and terminal differentiation under specific conditions
30
. Such an inherent capability of tumor cells to respond to environmental cues with molecular and phenotypic changes is reported as class switching in several cancers
26
,
28
,
31
.
The ID8 syngeneic mouse model is thus, a robust representation of Class 3/Mixed clinical HGSC subtype presenting the entire repertoire of phenotypic plasticity. Orthotopic primary tumors in the ovarian niche indicated to be in an iE state on metastasis to the peritoneum generate liquid tumor ascites which is in an iM state finally undergoes terminal differentiation into an epithelial (E) state in the solid tumors in secondary organs
30
. Our study thus recapitulates the reported class switching in HGSC patient tumors between the primary and metastatic tumor niches, due to self-renewal and trans-differentiation of cancer stem cells in the tumor mass
28
,
32
. However, we did not characterize in this study are multi-cellular spheroids (that have a higher capacity to avoid anoikis despite the shear pressure of peritoneal tumor ascites) which are likely to represent a differentiated ‘E’ state and serve as precursors of passive metastases to the secondary organs
33
.
Interestingly, different tumor sites develop a distinct TME along with modulated phenotypes, which is reported earlier
34
,
35
. Subcutaneous versus orthotropic TME reports differential levels of inflammatory cytokines like IL2 and IFN-ϒ, PD-L1, T cell populations (CD4/CD8 ratios) and macrophages that could reflect on a distinct repertoire of immune cell infiltration at different sites, some of which is already known
36
–
41
. While the intra-bursal tumors on the surface of ovary (site of disease origin) represent combination of pro-tumorigenic and anti-tumorigenic TME features the peripheral placement of TILs within these suggest immune exclusion
38
. Targeting of some of the associated molecular networks to convert the same into an immune responsive state could be an aim of therapy
42
. Our temporal profiling of the peritoneal ascites provided us with a rare glimpse of TME that changes subtly with disease progression wherein early disease (first tapping/tap1) presents an immune responsive phenotype with high frequency of infiltrating effector and cytotoxic T and other anti-tumorigenic cells that may mediate immune checkpoint inhibitor blockade. Tregs and MDSCs accumulate during tumor progression (Tap2 and Tap3) that render tumors less responsive for immunotherapy
43
–
46
. Surprisingly, the metastatic intestine displayed a high frequency of cytotoxic T cells
47
,
48
and PDL1 expression that again suggests responsiveness to immune checkpoint blockade. However, peritoneal cluster of tumors at that stage of disease is likely to compromise on organ function by sheer physical blockade of organ homeostasis, for which tumor cell targeting therapies may be irrelevant
49
,
50
.
This precise mapping of phenotype associated with distinct expression patterns and functions in a HGSC mouse model aligns well with clinical tumor subtypes, making it a reliable way to interpret experimental results. Conclusively, plasticity of a hybrid E/M tumor cell generates discrete tumor entities at different tissue niches that is associated not only with molecular tumor cell heterogeneity, but also a distinct TME
23
,
51
–
54
. This presents newer challenges in therapy and may well be the weak spot of HGSC.
Conclusion
Tumor heterogeneity in HGSC is the major bottleneck in developing targeted/personalized therapy hence, stratification of HGSC tumors is the approach to personalize treatment. ID8 syngeneic mouse model presents contrasting molecular and immune profiles of primary and secondary tumors that need to be considered while devising therapeutic interventions. Through this model we also establish that subcutaneous tumor models do not recapitulate the disease in its true sense as compared to orthotopic models.
